title: Why is this React component re-rendering and how would you prove the cause?
description: Learn to diagnose unnecessary React re-renders using Profiler, render-cause tracing, and component boundary refactoring. Covers reconciliation, memoization strategies, and common pitfalls.

data.text: Every React re-render has a cause, but the cause is not always obvious. A parent re-renders, a prop object reference changes, context value shifts, or state updates in a sibling. In a large codebase these chain together. Your job is to trace the chain to its origin and prove it with evidence—not guess.

React re-renders a component when its **state changes**, its **parent re-renders**, or the **context it consumes changes**. React then runs the component function again, diffs the result against the previous render, and patches the DOM. The diff step is cheap; the function execution is what you want to avoid if the output is unchanged.

terms.definition: React's algorithm for diffing a new render tree against the previous one and computing the minimal DOM mutations.
The phase where React calls component functions to produce React elements. It must be pure.
The phase where React applies computed changes to the DOM and runs layout effects.
For objects and functions, `a === b`. A new reference in a prop triggers re-render even if contents are identical.

data.title: High-frequency triggers
items: Inline object/array/function literals in JSX props—new reference every render
Context value created inline: `<Provider value={{ user }}>` causes all consumers to re-render on every parent render
Array methods like `.map()`, `.filter()`, `.sort()` inside render that produce new arrays
State in a parent that irrelevant children consume because the parent passes it down through props
Missing `key` on list items causing full re-mounts instead of in-place reordering

data.text: Start with the **React DevTools Profiler**. Record an interaction, then inspect the flamegraph. Every colored bar is a committed render. Click a bar to see **why** it rendered: props changed, state changed, hook changed, or parent rendered. This eliminates speculation.

data.title: Diagnosis workflow
items: Open Profiler, click Record, perform the action that feels slow
Find the component that renders too many times or takes too long
Check the 'Why did this render?' panel for the specific trigger
If it's 'parent rendered,' add a console.log to the parent and walk up the tree until you find the state change
If it's 'props changed,' use `useMemo` or stabilize the reference at the source
If it's 'hooks changed,' verify your dependency arrays and callback refs

data.title: Inline callback causing child re-renders
data.content: A parent re-renders on every keystroke and passes a new `onSave` function to a memoized child.

data.title: Fix: stabilize callback with useCallback
data.content: `useCallback` returns the same function reference across renders when dependencies haven't changed, letting `React.memo` do its job.

data.title: Premature memoization
data.text: Don't wrap every component in `React.memo` by default. Memoization itself has a cost—React must shallow-compare props on every parent render. Only memoize when profiling shows the child is expensive to render or renders excessively.

data.caption: How a state change flows through the React component tree

items: React DevTools Profiler: built-in flamegraph and render-cause inspection
`why-did-you-render` library: logs to console when a component re-renders and shows which prop changed
Chrome Performance tab: captures long tasks and JavaScript execution, useful when React isn't the bottleneck
`useWhyDidYouRender` hook: attach selectively to suspect components during investigation

data.text: A frequent root cause: state is hoisted to a shared ancestor, so any update triggers a re-render cascade through unrelated subtrees. The fix is usually **state colocation**: move state down to the lowest common ancestor of the components that actually use it, or split the component into independent branches.

data.title: Colocate state to avoid cascade
data.content: Before: filter state in a sidebar causes the main content area to re-render on every keystroke. After: extract a `FilterInput` component that owns its own local state.

items.question: What is the difference between React.memo and useMemo?
items.answer: `React.memo` is a component wrapper that skips re-rendering when props are shallow-equal. `useMemo` is a hook that memoizes a computed value. Use `memo` for component boundaries; use `useMemo` for expensive calculations you want to reuse across renders.

items.question: Can React.memo cause bugs?
items.answer: Yes. If you memoize a component that expects fresh objects (like event handlers that close over changing state), you may pass stale references. Always verify memoization is actually helping with the Profiler before committing to it.

items.question: Does React re-render when you call setState with the same value?
items.answer: For primitive state (string, number), React bails out if the value is the same via Object.is comparison. For objects and arrays, it bails out only if the reference is identical—even if the contents are deeply equal.

items.question: What about context providers that re-render all consumers?
items.answer: Any context consumer re-renders when the provider value reference changes. Split contexts by concern (e.g., separate auth, theme, and feature contexts) and memoize provider values with `useMemo`.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Start with React DevTools Profiler—let it show you the render cause instead of guessing
Inline object/function literals in JSX create new references every render
Use React.memo only after profiling shows a child renders too often
Colocate state to the lowest common ancestor to limit cascade scope
data.takeaway: Proving a re-render cause is a trace, not a guess. Profile first, refactor second.
